explanations.answer: Gather them down into one valley
explanations.explanation: That's what He says. “I will gather all the nations and bring them down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat.” (Joel 3:2) Every nation is on the guest list, and nobody gets to say they had other plans.

explanations.answer: Send them all home in peace
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The LORD says He will “gather all the nations and bring them down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat.” (Joel 3:2) The restoring in verse 1 is for Judah and Jerusalem, and the nations get called to the valley instead of being sent home.

Close, but scattering is something the nations did. The LORD says Israel is the one “whom they have scattered among the nations.” (Joel 3:2) What He does with the nations is gather them. I once tried to scatter flour across the counter, and it didn't end well either.

explanations.answer: How they treated His people Israel
explanations.explanation: Right on target. He says, “There I will enter into judgment against them concerning My people, My inheritance, Israel…” (Joel 3:2) The judgment is about what was done to His people. That's the whole case, friend.

explanations.answer: How they treated their own kings
explanations.explanation: Not this time. The LORD says the judgment is “concerning My people, My inheritance, Israel…” (Joel 3:2) Nothing in the passage mentions the nations' kings. The charges are about what they did to Israel.

explanations.answer: How they ran their trade routes
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the text never brings up trade routes. The LORD says the judgment is “concerning My people, My inheritance, Israel…” (Joel 3:2) Everything He lists after that is about what was done to His people and His land.

True. The LORD says Israel was scattered “as they divided up My land.” (Joel 3:2) He calls it His. He calls the people His too, His inheritance. So the nations weren't just splitting up some empty ground.
It's true, friend. Joel 3:2 has the LORD saying Israel was scattered “as they divided up My land.” It's right there in His own words. The nations divided up something that was His.

Not this one. The LORD says, “I will swiftly and speedily return your recompense upon your heads.” (Joel 3:4) That's the opposite of taking His time. If I moved that fast, the cookies would be out of the oven before I turned it on.

False it is. He says that if they retaliate, “I will swiftly and speedily return your recompense upon your heads.” (Joel 3:4) No slow rolling and no waiting around. When He says swiftly, He means swiftly.

Yes, the Greeks. The LORD says, “You sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks, to send them far from their homeland.” (Joel 3:6) The point was to send them far away. I think that's a hard thing to read.

Not here, friend. Joel 3:6 says they sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem “to the Greeks.” Egypt does come up later in the passage, but it's in verse 19, when its land is left desolate. Verse 6 is about the Greeks.

Babylon is a famous name, but it's not in this passage. The LORD says they sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem “to the Greeks, to send them far from their homeland.” (Joel 3:6) This verse names the Greeks, so that's where the people were sent.

explanations.answer: They'll be sold to the people of Judah
explanations.explanation: That's what He says. “I will sell your sons and daughters into the hands of the people of Judah…” (Joel 3:8) The same thing they did to Judah comes back around to them, which is what He meant by returning it on their heads.

explanations.answer: They'll be carried off to Damascus
explanations.explanation: Damascus isn't in this passage. The LORD says, “I will sell your sons and daughters into the hands of the people of Judah…” (Joel 3:8) So the sons and daughters go into the hands of the people of Judah.

explanations.answer: They'll be sent away to Cush
explanations.explanation: Cush never shows up in these verses. The LORD says, “I will sell your sons and daughters into the hands of the people of Judah…” (Joel 3:8) The people of Judah are the ones who receive them. After that, the people of Judah sell them on to a distant nation.
The Sabeans, yes. The LORD says the people of Judah “will sell them to the Sabeans…” and calls them a distant nation. (Joel 3:8) The far-off buyer is the one named in the text.
Moabites don't appear in this passage. Verse 8 says the people of Judah “will sell them to the Sabeans…” and calls them a distant nation. (Joel 3:8) Sabeans is the name to hold onto, friend.

Assyrians are a well-known name, but Joel 3 doesn't use it. The LORD says the people of Judah “will sell them to the Sabeans…” and calls them a distant nation. (Joel 3:8) The Sabeans are the people He names.

That's the call. “Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears.” (Joel 3:10) Tools made for farming get turned into tools for war. If somebody did that to my cookie stamper, I'd need a long sit-down.
No burying here. The message is, “Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears.” (Joel 3:10) The farm tools get put to a whole new use. Nobody is digging holes in this verse.

No horse trading in this passage, friend. The text says, “Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears.” (Joel 3:10) The plowshares and pruning hooks themselves get reshaped into weapons.

Sit down, that's the one. “…for there I will sit down to judge all the nations on every side.” (Joel 3:12) The nations rush to the valley, and He is the one who sits down to judge them. I'll leave it at what the text says.
Not quite. The LORD says, “…for there I will sit down to judge all the nations on every side.” (Joel 3:12) The word is sit, friend. It's a small word, but it's the one in the verse.

Marching is what the nations are told to do. They are called to advance to the Valley of Jehoshaphat. About the LORD, the verse says, “…there I will sit down to judge all the nations on every side.” (Joel 3:12)

Yes, that's the reason given. “…the wine vats overflow because their wickedness is great.” (Joel 3:13) The picture is a winepress packed to the brim. It's a serious verse, friend, so I'll let it stand.

Rain isn't mentioned anywhere in this passage. The verse says, “…the wine vats overflow because their wickedness is great.” (Joel 3:13) The overflow comes from the nations' wickedness, not the weather.
The text doesn't say anything about early or late. It does say the harvest is ripe. Then it gives the reason for the overflow: “…the wine vats overflow because their wickedness is great.” (Joel 3:13)
Near is the word. “For the Day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision.” (Joel 3:14) Not far off, not already past. Near.
Not over, friend. The verse says, “For the Day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision.” (Joel 3:14) The crowds are still gathering in the valley, so the Day is close but hasn't finished.
Delayed isn't in the verse. Joel 3:14 says, “For the Day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision.” Near is the word the text uses.
True. “The sun and moon will grow dark, and the stars will no longer shine.” (Joel 3:15) Even the lights in the sky go dim. I'm only telling you what the verse says, friend.
It's true, friend. Joel 3:15 says, “The sun and moon will grow dark, and the stars will no longer shine.” That is what the prophecy says about the sky. I'll just leave it at that.

That's it. “But the LORD will be a refuge for His people, a stronghold for the people of Israel.” (Joel 3:16) Heaven and earth are trembling, and still He is a refuge and a stronghold for His people. That's a comfort.

explanations.answer: A judge watching from far away
explanations.explanation: Not far away at all. The text says, “The LORD will roar from Zion and raise His voice from Jerusalem…” (Joel 3:16) Then it says, “But the LORD will be a refuge for His people, a stronghold for the people of Israel.” He's not watching from a distance, friend.

explanations.answer: A voice they can no longer hear
explanations.explanation: Quite the opposite, friend. “The LORD will roar from Zion and raise His voice from Jerusalem…” (Joel 3:16) That's a voice raised loud, and for His own people He is “a refuge” and “a stronghold.”
Not this time. The LORD says, “Jerusalem will be holy, never again to be overrun by foreigners.” (Joel 3:17) The word is never again. That's a promise, friend.
False, you got it. “Jerusalem will be holy, never again to be overrun by foreigners.” (Joel 3:17) Never again means never again. Even I can't find a loophole in that one.

Right from the house of the LORD. “…a spring will flow from the house of the LORD to water the Valley of Acacias.” (Joel 3:18) The water starts at His house and goes out from there. Mighty fine plumbing, friend.

That's the valley of judgment, and it's not where this spring starts. The verse says, “…a spring will flow from the house of the LORD to water the Valley of Acacias.” (Joel 3:18) The water begins at the LORD's house.

Edom gets no spring in this passage. In fact, Edom is called “a desert wasteland” (Joel 3:19). The spring comes from somewhere else, because Joel 3:18 says, “…a spring will flow from the house of the LORD to water the Valley of Acacias.”

explanations.answer: Because of their violence against Judah
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the reason the text gives. Egypt and Edom will be desolate “because of the violence done to the people of Judah, in whose land they shed innocent blood.” (Joel 3:19) It's a heavy verse, and I won't make light of it.

explanations.answer: Because they turned Judah's messengers away
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about messengers. It gives this reason: “because of the violence done to the people of Judah, in whose land they shed innocent blood.” (Joel 3:19) That's the reason for Egypt and Edom, and it's a heavy one.

explanations.answer: Because their own rivers dried up
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention their rivers at all. It says Egypt and Edom will be desolate “because of the violence done to the people of Judah, in whose land they shed innocent blood.” (Joel 3:19) The reason comes from what was done to Judah, friend.

Forever, that's the word. “But Judah will be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem from generation to generation.” (Joel 3:20) Egypt and Edom end up desolate, but Judah stays lived in. A long, long time, friend.

Briefly would be a short stay, and that's not what the text says. “But Judah will be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem from generation to generation.” (Joel 3:20) Forever is a whole lot longer than a quick visit.

That one is the reverse of what the verse says. “But Judah will be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem from generation to generation.” (Joel 3:20) It's Egypt and Edom that are left desolate, friend. Judah stays inhabited.
